questions.q: In water-gas shift reaction, hydrogen gas is produced from the reaction of steam with.
questions.solution:
Water-gas shift reaction is
$CO + {H}_{2}OFeO \cdot {Cr}_{2}{O}_{3} ( Catalyst ) > {CO}_{2} + {H}_{2}$
In this reaction, hydrogen gas is produced from the reaction of steam with carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Strength of a ${H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution is labeled as $1. 79N$. Its strength can also be expressed as closest to
questions.solution:
$2{H}_{2}{O}_{2   \left(aq.\right)} ⟶ 2{H}_{2}O \left(ℓ\right) + ${O}_{2}$\left(g\right)$

General Solution :- 

It is a common trend that $n$-factor $\left({H}_{2}{O}_{2}\right)is
taken as '2$' 

By the definition of volume strength of ${H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ if we consume $1ℓ of 1N{H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ in the above equation we are using 1 gram equivalent of
${H}_{2}{O}_{2} ≡ 0. 5$ moles of ${H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ (by using $n$-factor $= 2$)

This will produce $\dfrac{1}{4}  moles$ of {O}_{2}$ gas at $N. T. P. ≡ $\dfrac{1}{4}$\times22. 4 = 5. 6ℓ$ of {O}_{2} gas

i.e. $1ℓ, 1N{H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution gives $5. 6ℓ {O}_{2}$ at $N. T. P$

Hence $1N ≡ 5. 6$ 'vol.' ${H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution

In the given question it is $1. 76N{H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution Hence volume strength $= 5. 6 \times1. 79 ≃ 10$ volumes

Suggested Solution& :-& 

$2{H}_{2}{O}_{2  $\left(aq.\right)$} ⟶ 2{H}_{2}O  $\left(ℓ\right) +   {O}_{2}\left(g\right)$ The above equation is a classic example of
disproportionation of{H}_{2}{O}_{2}, hence we should taken$-factor of ${H}_{2}{O}_{2} = 1$

1ℓ, 1N{H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution $≡ 1Gm$ equivalent of ${H}_{2}{O}_{2} ≡ 1$ mole of ${H}_{2}{O}_{2}$

This will produce $\dfrac{1}{2} moles$ of {O}_{2}$ gas at $N. T. P. = $\dfrac{1}{2}\times22. 4 = 11. 2ℓ$ of {O}_{2} gas

i.e. 1ℓ, 1N{H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution gives 11. 2ℓ of {O}_{2}$ gas at $N. T. P.$

Hence 1N ≡ 11. 2$ 'vol' ${H}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution 

In the given question it is $1. 79{NH}_{2}{O}_{2}$ solution

Hence, volume strength $= 1. 79 \times11. 2 ≃ 10$ volumes

Suggested Answer is option (A)$

questions.q: Permanent hardness of water can be removed by&
questions.solution:
Sodium hexametaphosphate $\left({Na}_{6}{P}_{4}{O}_{18}\right)$ (or Calgon) coverts ${Ca}^{2 +}$ and
${Mg}^{2 +}$ ions in water (which~ cause hardness) into a soluble complex.&

${Na}_{6}{P}_{6}{O}_{18} ⟶ 2{Na}^{+} + {Na}_{4}{P}_{6}{O}_{18}^{2 -}$

${Ca}^{2 +} + {Na}_{4}{P}_{6}{O}_{18}^{2 -} ⟶ 2{Na}^{+} + {CaNa}_{2}{P}_{6}{O}_{18}^{2 -}$
